title: Hezekiah's Prayer and Jerusalem's Deliverance
summary: Hezekiah goes to the temple in sackcloth and sends to the prophet Isaiah, who tells him not to fear. Sennacherib sends a second threat in a letter, and Hezekiah spreads it before the LORD and prays that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that the LORD alone is God. Isaiah answers with a long oracle against the Assyrian king's pride, a promise that a remnant will survive, and a pledge that Sennacherib will not enter the city. That night the angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp, Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, and years later he is killed by his own sons.
story: Chapter 18 ended with the Rabshakeh's challenge hanging in the air: which god has ever rescued his land from Assyria, and how could the LORD rescue Jerusalem? This chapter answers. It is the high point of Hezekiah's reign and one of the great deliverance stories of the Old Testament, set deliberately against the fall of Samaria two chapters earlier. Samaria trusted other gods and was taken; Jerusalem, under a king who prays, is spared. Yet the reader of Kings knows that the reprieve is not permanent. Chapter 20 will close with Isaiah's warning that Babylon will one day carry off Jerusalem's treasures, and chapters 21 to 25 tell how that happened. This chapter shows what trust in the LORD could do, and what Judah would later lose.
historical:
The events belong to Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC. Libnah (verse 8) was a town in the lowlands near Lachish. Tirhakah (Taharqa in Egyptian sources) was a king of the Cushite dynasty that ruled Egypt from Nubia, the region south of Egypt the Bible calls Cush. He became pharaoh around 690 BC, so many scholars think the title king is used here in anticipation, for the prince who led the Egyptian force in 701; others propose that the text combines two Assyrian campaigns, a view that has not won wide acceptance. Sennacherib's own annals report a battle with an Egyptian and Cushite army at Eltekeh and claim victory.

The annals say that Hezekiah was shut up in Jerusalem and paid tribute, but they never claim the city was taken, an unusual silence in Assyrian royal inscriptions. The Greek historian Herodotus preserves an Egyptian story that Sennacherib's army was forced to retreat after mice overran its camp in the night, which some have connected with verse 35, though the link is uncertain. Sennacherib's death is confirmed in Babylonian records, which say he was killed by a son in a rebellion in 681 BC, about twenty years after this campaign; Esarhaddon, another son, then took the throne. Kings compresses those two decades into a single verse. The god Nisroch has not been identified with certainty.
cultural:
Tearing clothes and putting on sackcloth, a rough cloth of goat hair, were the ordinary signs of grief and repentance in Israel. Hezekiah's image in verse 3 of children come to birth with no strength to deliver them was a proverbial picture of utter helplessness at the decisive moment. Spreading the letter out before the LORD in the temple is a gesture of bringing the threat into the presence of the true king. Hezekiah addresses the LORD as enthroned between the cherubim, the winged figures over the ark of the covenant in the temple's inner room, which Israel understood as the footstool of God's invisible throne.

Assyrian kings boasted in their inscriptions of the kinds of feats listed in verses 23-24: crossing mountains with chariots, cutting cedars in Lebanon, digging wells in foreign lands. Isaiah's oracle turns their own style of self-praise against them. The punishment in verse 28, a hook in the nose and a bit in the mouth, uses an image of leading captives or animals; Assyrian art shows prisoners led by ropes attached to their faces. Isaiah turns the empire's own treatment of the conquered back on its king.
literary: The chapter mirrors chapter 18. There a threat was delivered and the people were silent; here a threat arrives again, and this time Hezekiah answers, not to the Assyrians but to the LORD. The chapter has two cycles of threat and response: the Rabshakeh's words lead to Hezekiah's appeal to Isaiah and a brief oracle (verses 1-7), and Sennacherib's letter leads to Hezekiah's prayer and a long oracle (verses 8-34). The prayer in verses 15-19 is a model of Old Testament prayer: it begins with who God is (creator and king of all the kingdoms), states the situation honestly, and asks for rescue for the sake of God's name among the nations. The oracle in verses 21-28 is poetry, a taunt song in which the despised city mocks the conqueror. The chapter closes with brief narrative that fulfills the promises exactly: the rumor, the return, the sword.

outline.t: Hezekiah turns to Isaiah; do not be afraid
A sign, a remnant, and a defended city
The Assyrian camp struck and Sennacherib's end

doctrines.note: Hezekiah's prayer grounds its request in God's character and aims at God's glory, asking for rescue so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that the LORD alone is God. The LORD answers explicitly because Hezekiah prayed (verse 20).

Isaiah tells Sennacherib that his conquests were planned by the LORD long ago (verse 25). The empire was a tool in God's hand, and its pride in its own strength was a failure to see who really ruled history.

Against the Rabshakeh's claim that the LORD is one local god among many, Hezekiah confesses him as the living God, creator of heaven and earth, while the gods of the nations were wood and stone. The chapter's outcome vindicates that confession.

words.note: Chay, living. Twice the Assyrians are said to defy the living God (verses 4 and 16). The title sets the LORD against the gods Assyria had burned, which were only wood and stone. A living God hears, sees, and acts, which is exactly what Hezekiah asks him to do.

Charaph, to taunt, reproach, or defy. It is the word used when Goliath defied the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:26). The echo is fitting: once again a giant of the nations mocks Israel's God, and once again the outcome is the reverse of what he expected.

Sheerit, remnant, what is left over. Hezekiah asks for prayer for the remnant (verse 4), and Isaiah promises that a remnant will go out from Jerusalem and take root again (verses 30-31). The remnant is one of Isaiah's great themes: God's promise is carried forward not by the whole nation but by the survivors he preserves.

christ: The oracle's promise of a remnant that takes root below and bears fruit above (verse 30) belongs to a larger hope in Isaiah, who also speaks of a shoot from the stump of Jesse, David's father (Isaiah 11:1). The New Testament sees that hope realized in Jesus, the descendant of David, and Paul quotes Isaiah's remnant promises in Romans 9:27-29 and 11:5 to explain how God keeps his word through a faithful remnant. Verse 34 says the LORD will defend Jerusalem for his own sake and for the sake of his servant David; the line of David survives because of God's promise, and it is from that line that the Messiah comes. Hezekiah's prayer that all kingdoms would know the LORD alone is God also anticipates the mission of the church, sent by the risen Christ to make disciples of all nations.

hard.q: Did the angel of the LORD really kill 185,000 Assyrians in one night, and how should we think about it?
hard.a:
Readers take verse 35 in several ways. Many accept it as a direct act of God, as the text plainly presents it. Others, who also accept that God acted, suggest that he did so through a sudden epidemic in the camp, noting that the angel of the LORD is linked with plague elsewhere (2 Samuel 24:15-16). Some scholars question the size of the number, since the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a military unit, which would make the figure smaller. What is historically secure is that Sennacherib did not take Jerusalem, that his own records claim only tribute, and that he returned to Assyria.

The moral question is real, since the deaths were of soldiers who carried out their king's orders. The text presents the event as judgment on an empire that had destroyed nation after nation and blasphemed God, and as the defense of a people who had no other help. It does not invite celebration of the dead, and its focus stays on the arrogance of the king who sent them.

questions: Hezekiah spread the threatening letter out before the LORD. What would it look like for you to bring a specific fear into God's presence in the same way?
Hezekiah asked for rescue so that the nations would know who God is. How might praying for God's reputation, and not only your relief, change your prayers?
Sennacherib thought his victories were his own achievement. Where do you take credit for what God has given?
